summary: Describes interoperability scenarios for using Provider Backbone Bridge functionality in Hierarchical VPLS, with Ethernet or MPLS access, to improve scalability in customer MAC addresses and service instances. It is informational rather than a new protocol.

eli5.summary: It shows how two different network styles can be snapped together so many more customers can fit.

subtitle: How Provider Backbone Bridging can be combined with H-VPLS to scale MAC addresses and service instances.

tldr.problem: H-VPLS learns customer MAC addresses and needs many pseudowires, and 802.1ad access networks are limited to 4094 service instances.
tldr.mechanism: Add Provider Backbone Bridge (IEEE 802.1ah) functions in the access network, the U-PE or the N-PE, so the VPLS side sees provider MAC addresses and a 24-bit I-SID identifies each service.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes interoperability and migration scenarios and their trade-offs, without defining a new protocol.

today: RFC 7080 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes scenarios and trade-offs rather than a new protocol.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem
sections.content:
RFC 4762 describes two-tier Hierarchical VPLS (H-VPLS) with MPLS access or IEEE 802.1ad (QinQ) Ethernet access. In both, forwarding is based on customer MAC addresses (C-MACs), which becomes a problem as the number of VPLS instances grows. The number of pseudowires (PWs) at N-PE devices also grows with the number of customer service instances times the number of N-PEs in the full mesh.

An 802.1ad access network adds another limit: each S-VLAN represents a service instance and there are only 4094 S-VLANs. RFC 6246 highlights these issues. This document shows how IEEE 802.1ah, Provider Backbone Bridges (PBB), can be integrated with H-VPLS to address them.
sections.eli5: The old system made every router remember every customer's address and gave out only a few thousand labels. PBB fixes both.

sections.title: PBB Access: Domains and Service Interfaces
sections.content:
With PBB, customer frames are wrapped in a provider header, so the VPLS PE sees only the provider's backbone MAC addresses (B-MACs). The 24-bit I-SID allows up to 16M services per PBB access network, compared with 4094 per 802.1Q/802.1ad network. It also separates the service layer (I-SID) from the network layer (B-VLAN).

The RFC defines three kinds of service domain. In a Tightly Coupled domain, PBBNs share the same I-SID and B-VLAN domain. In a Loosely Coupled domain they share I-SIDs but have independent B-VLANs, so I-SIDs must be remapped to B-VIDs. In Different Service Domains each has its own I-SID and B-VLAN space, so I-SID translation is needed too.

A VPLS-PE connecting to a PBBN uses one of two service interfaces. Type I is B-tagged with the B-VID as service delimiter; the PE treats frames as 802.1ad frames and needs no PBB functions. Type II is I-tagged with the I-SID as delimiter; the PE includes the B-BEB function.
sections.eli5: Customer mail goes into labeled envelopes. The post office only reads the outer address, and the label inside says which customer it belongs to.

sections.title: Type I, Type II and Mixed Access
sections.content:
Type I suits Tightly Coupled domains and needs nothing new on the PE. Its advantage is that many I-SIDs share one full-mesh PW, saving PWs and avoiding C-MACs in the core. Its disadvantage is more replication, since unknown unicast, multicast or broadcast on one service floods the whole core mesh. This can be reduced with flood containment per I-SID (B-MAC multicast pruning). Port, VLAN and VLAN bundling modes use Ethernet raw mode (0x0005) PWs, with tagged mode (0x0004) possible for VLAN mode.

Type II suits Loosely Coupled and Different Service Domains. Operators can choose a full mesh of PWs per I-SID, per group of I-SIDs or for all I-SIDs, trading PW state against flood containment.

When a PBN (802.1ad) access network meets a PBBN, either the PBN-side PE is modified to include IB-BEB functions, with S-VIDs mapped one to one onto I-SIDs and I-SID bundling supported, or a regular PBN PE is kept and the PBBN-side PE does the mapping. In that second case, I-SID bundling mode is not supported.
sections.eli5: You can share one big road for many customers, which saves roads but is noisy, or build separate roads per group, which is quieter but costs more.

sections.title: PBB with MPLS Access
sections.content:
For H-VPLS with MPLS access, PBB functions can sit in the U-PE or the N-PE. In ordinary H-VPLS the N-PE must learn the C-MACs of all its VPLS instances, possibly hundreds of thousands or millions. With PBB on the U-PE, the N-PE learns only the U-PE MAC addresses.

The U-PE keeps offering port, VLAN and VLAN-bundling services, but maps each customer's service onto a single I-SID. Many I-SIDs are multiplexed in one bridge domain (B-VLAN), mapped to one VPLS instance, and N-PEs forward on B-MACs and B-VID without looking at I-SIDs. The fewer PWs come at the cost of more replication, which flood containment per I-SID remedies.

When PBB is on the N-PE instead, the spoke PW from the U-PE is not service multiplexed: one service per PW. The N-PE maps services onto I-SIDs and then either one I-SID or a whole bridge domain to a VPLS instance.
sections.eli5: Put the envelope-stuffing at the edge, and the middle of the network only needs to remember a handful of addresses.

sections.title: Migration Scenarios
sections.content:
Operators are unlikely to migrate to PBB overnight, so three scenarios let existing MPLS access networks coexist with new PBB ones.

  • 802.1ad frames over the core (7.1): existing networks stay unchanged and the new network's N-PE terminates PBB before the core. No change to existing PEs, but no PBB scalability gains for them.
  • PBB frames over the core (7.2): better MAC and PW scalability, but all existing N-PEs must be upgraded with IB-BEB functions.
  • Mixed (7.3): existing networks use 802.1ad and new ones exchange PBB frames, with the new N-PE doing both B-BEB and IB-BEB functions. It combines the advantages but needs new N-PE functionality and two P2MP LSPs at the ingress N-PE. PEs must learn each peer's capability by static configuration or by extending the control plane as in RFC 6074, which is out of scope.
sections.eli5: You can leave old neighbourhoods alone, convert everything at once, or let both styles live together. The last choice is best but needs smarter gateways.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no security aspects beyond those that apply to VPLS and H-VPLS. Those are already covered in RFC 4111 and RFC 4762.

Readers should look there for the relevant threats and protections.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about; the old safety rules still apply.

All existing N-PEs must be upgraded
